claims.text: A uniform nanoscale metallic coating on tungsten particles reduces electron scattering at the tungsten–copper interface.
Reducing electron scattering at the tungsten–copper interface increases the composite's thermal conductivity.
The metallic interfacial coating does not degrade the mechanical durability of the W–Cu composite.
The metallic interfacial coating does not degrade the irradiation resistance of the W–Cu composite.
Fusion-reactor operating conditions involve thermal-management demands and neutron irradiation.
A nanoscale metallic coating enhances bonding between tungsten particles and the copper matrix.
A nanoscale metallic coating limits the formation of deleterious defects at the tungsten–copper interface.
Poor interface quality can reduce the properties of metal-matrix composites.
Improved tungsten–copper interfacial bonding enables more efficient electron transport across the interface.
More efficient electron transport lowers tungsten–copper interfacial thermal resistance.
Lower tungsten–copper interfacial resistance boosts the overall thermal conductivity of the composite.
Keeping the coating thin preserves tungsten's mechanical strength.
Keeping the coating thin preserves tungsten's irradiation stability.
Relative to an otherwise equivalent uncoated W–Cu composite, the coated composite will have measurably higher thermal conductivity.
Relative to an otherwise equivalent uncoated W–Cu composite, the coated composite will retain similar mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
The proposed benefit depends on producing a uniform and adherent nanoscale coating without introducing new phases or defects.
Variations in coating material, thickness, and processing conditions may alter the magnitude of the thermal-conductivity improvement.
